commentary.bottom_line: Seven sources, one framework and six commentaries, recommend consulting experts, community members, and people with knowledge of patient experience when assessing AI bias, but no supplied study tests whether this consultation detects bias or reduces inequity. The recommendation currently rests on expert opinion and on the reasoning that affected groups can surface concerns developers miss.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests stakeholder or community consultation as a bias-assessment method, and no study documents the hazard itself. The seven endorsements consist of the CHAI framework and six commentaries, all phrased as should statements. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement of this kind does not establish certainty about effect, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence.

Several endorsing commentaries argue that community members and social researchers can identify historical bias in data sources and variables. None of the supplied sources reports a test of this claim in any population. Health systems therefore cannot yet say which consultation methods, if any, reach Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients well enough to change what bias assessments find.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares bias assessments conducted with and without input from community members, patients, or subject matter experts. Useful designs would measure whether consultation identifies biases or baseline inequities that technical audits alone miss, whether those findings change model design or deployment decisions, and what consultation costs in staff time and participant compensation. Studies should also specify who was consulted, how they were recruited, and how their input was recorded and acted upon.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Because these groups are often the intended voices in community consultation, the absence of tests means health systems have no data on whether consultation methods actually reach them or reflect their concerns.
